section_title: How do Deborah and Barak respond to God’s command?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 After Ehud died, the Israelites again did evil in the sight of the LORD. 2 So the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his forces was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim. 3 Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, because Jabin had nine hundred chariots of iron, and he had harshly oppressed the Israelites for twenty years.

4 Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. 5 And she would sit under the Palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, where the Israelites would go up to her for judgment. 6 She summoned Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and said to him, “Surely the LORD, the God of Israel, is commanding you: ‘Go and march to Mount Tabor, taking with you ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun. 7 And I will draw out Sisera the commander of Jabin’s army, his chariots, and his troops to the River Kishon, and I will deliver him into your hand.’”

8 Barak said to her, “If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.” 9 “I will certainly go with you,” Deborah replied, “but the road you are taking will bring you no honor, because the LORD will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman.” So Deborah got up and went with Barak to Kedesh, 10 where he summoned Zebulun and Naphtali. Ten thousand men followed him, and Deborah also went with him. 11 Now Heber the Kenite had moved away from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent by the great tree of Zaanannim, which was near Kedesh.

12 When Sisera was told that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up Mount Tabor, 13 he summoned all nine hundred of his iron chariots and all the men with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the River Kishon. 14 Then Deborah said to Barak, “Arise, for this is the day that the LORD has delivered Sisera into your hand. Has not the LORD gone before you?” So Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men following him. 15 And in front of him the LORD routed with the sword Sisera, all his charioteers, and all his army. Sisera abandoned his chariot and fled on foot. 16 Then Barak pursued the chariots and army as far as Harosheth-hagoyim, and the whole army of Sisera fell by the sword; not a single man was left.

context_lines: After Ehud dies, Israel again turns to evil. Jabin of Hazor and his commander Sisera oppress the people for twenty years, supported by nine hundred iron chariots. The Israelites cry to the LORD, and the account introduces Deborah, who is already serving as a prophetess and judge. People come to her to have their disputes heard.

The Hebrew title נְבִיאָה, *neviah* (neh-vee-AH), means prophetess; [Brown–Driver–Briggs](https://biblehub.com/hebrew/5031.htm) lists Deborah alongside other women called by that title. Here she communicates the LORD’s command and promise to Barak: gather the troops, go to Mount Tabor, and God will bring Sisera to the Kishon and give him into Barak’s hand.

Barak agrees to go only if Deborah goes with him. She consents, while announcing that the honor attached to Sisera’s defeat will go to a woman. Barak gathers the men, and when Deborah announces the time to act, he leads them down the mountain. The account credits the LORD with routing Sisera’s forces while also describing Barak’s pursuit. Sisera himself escapes on foot, setting up the next scene.

The brief notice about Heber’s move near Kedesh introduces the household that will become important when Sisera seeks shelter. It belongs to the unfolding account, even though its significance is not yet explained.
common_interpretation_lines: Readers recognize Deborah’s significant place in God’s rescue. The [Catholic Catechism, paragraph 64](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_one/chapter_two/article_1/ii_the_stages_of_revelation.index.html), includes her among the holy women who kept Israel’s hope of salvation alive. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/4.htm) describes her as speaking God’s message and administering justice, while [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-judges/) emphasizes the authority the people acknowledged in her judging and summoning Barak.

The emphasis differs when readers assess Barak’s condition. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-judges/) sees both genuine faith in his willingness to go and weakness in his refusal to go without Deborah. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/4.htm) also acknowledges weakness but gives more attention to his desire for her counsel, prayer, and reassuring presence. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/4.htm) highlights Deborah’s willingness to share the danger and Barak’s concern for the mission’s success over his personal honor. These are readings of his response; his private thoughts are not fully narrated.
god_plan_lines: The New Testament explicitly includes Barak among people remembered for faith. [Hebrews 11:32–34](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/11.htm) names him in its account of God strengthening people in weakness and giving victories through faith. His need for encouragement does not erase the faith shown when he acts.

Hebrews then leads beyond these earlier servants to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith, who endured the cross and is seated at God’s right hand ([Hebrews 12:1–3](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/12.htm)). The larger story honors God’s work through people such as Deborah and Barak while directing our lasting hope and attention to Christ.
